title: Behavior Mixing with Minimum Global and Subgroup Connectivity Maintenance for Large-Scale Multi-Robot Systems
venue: 2020 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
evidence: Sec. II/III (Eqs. 3,6,7-9): at each time step a QP minimises sum ||u_i - u_hat_i||^2 subject to pairwise safety and connectivity barrier constraints on the selected spanning-tree edges, so 'the robots controllers are minimally modified from the original controllers' (Conclusion).
method: Distributed real-time Minimum Connectivity Constraint Spanning Tree selects fewest inter-robot links to keep team and subgroups connected; safety/connectivity barrier certificates then minimally modify subgroup nominal controllers via QP.
evaluation: Simulation only, 40-100 unicycle robots in 4 behaviour subgroups; baselines: fixed initial MST and fixed initial graph constraints; metrics: min inter-robot distance vs 0.02 m, algebraic connectivity, control perturbation, target distance, MCCST messages/time (figures only).
contribution: A distributed minimum-connectivity spanning tree chooses the least-restrictive link constraints so barrier-certificate QPs keep large heterogeneous robot teams connected and collision-free with minimal controller perturbation.
flag: Barrier-certificate QP is a runtime filter in form, but the contribution and measured outcomes are connectivity maintenance and control perturbation; collision avoidance is a standard side constraint from prior work, so primacy test for (c) fails.

title: Collision Avoidance Based on Robust Lexicographic Task Assignment
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
evidence: Sec. IV-B/V: time-varying position bounds derived from the robust bottleneck assignment are computed offline from initial positions, destinations and a timing parameter; the paper says it 'is enough to tune or design the controllers for every agent individually such that the deviations ... do not violate the local constraints' and describes no runtime enforcement.
method: Lexicographic (sequential) bottleneck task assignment with a robustness margin yields per-agent time-varying position bounds that, if respected by individual controllers, provably exclude inter-agent collisions.
evaluation: Single illustrative simulation: 8 unicycle robots, 6 destinations, s=3 m, mu=9.02 m, disturbed steering; no baselines, no collision counts or clearance statistics; complexity O(m n^3), no wall-clock timing.
contribution: Robust lexicographic bottleneck assignment produces decoupled per-agent position bounds that guarantee multi-agent collision avoidance without inter-agent position sharing.
flag: Planning-time guarantee, no runtime interception; collision avoidance is the stated claim but there is no measured hazard outcome or baseline (also E2).

title: Combining Control Barrier Functions and Behavior Trees for Multi-Agent Underwater Coverage Missions
venue: 2020 59th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. IV-B (Eq. 8): the nominal control k(x) of each behaviour-tree action is projected by a minimally disturbing CBF-QP onto controls that keep all higher-priority conditions invariant, dropping lowest-priority constraints when infeasible for 'graceful performance degradation'.
method: Concurrent-Goals Behavior Tree whose conditions are control barrier functions; each ticked action's controller is filtered by a prioritised CBF-QP so safety, battery and connectivity constraints are maintained during phase switches.
evaluation: Simulation only: 3 kinematic AUVs in a coverage mission with unknown obstacles; qualitative comparison of reactive control, unconstrained BT and CBF-BT; no collision/connectivity counts, success rates, hardware or compute time.
contribution: Combines control barrier functions with behavior trees so prioritised safety, battery and connectivity constraints filter each action's controller during a simulated three-AUV coverage mission.
flag: Runtime CBF filter over BT actions fits (a) and the setting is multi-agent, but the evaluation is a single qualitative trajectory; Lemma 1 assumptions admitted not to hold in the AUV example.

title: Decentralized Goal Assignment and Safe Trajectory Generation in Multirobot Networks via Multiple Lyapunov Functions
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control
evidence: Sec. V-B/C: agents run the optimal goal assignment (OGA) policy, monitor the barrier-based function Q_i (Eq. 21), and when Q_i > 0 switch via hysteresis to the Last-Resort control law (Eq. 22) that renders trajectories collision-free; the LR policy 'will be active only when the OGA policy is about to result in colliding trajectories' (Problem 3).
method: Decentralized goal assignment via Lyapunov-like functions among locally connected robots, with a switched last-resort logarithmic-barrier controller that takes over at runtime when the assignment would lead to collision.
evaluation: Readable version: one N=10 simulation, min clearance always positive, LR policy active 21% of time, no baselines/ablation, estimated 1e-7 N^3 s planning time. v3/TAC abstract claims six-ground-robot experiments, not verifiable here.
contribution: A switched last-resort barrier controller overrides decentralized optimal goal assignment only when collisions are imminent, with proven stability and safety for locally communicating robot teams.
flag: Full text of v3 (TAC 2020) could not be read: arxiv.org/html and /pdf (v3 explicitly) both returned the 2014 v1 text (different title, N=10 sim only, no six-robot experiments, no baselines). Mechanism meets (a) on v1; evaluation floor (baseline/ablation) unverifiable, would be exclude-E2 on v1 evidence.

title: Decentralized Safe Reactive Planning under TWTL Specifications
venue: 2020 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Collision avoidance is enforced by pruning conflicting states/transitions inside each agent's receding-horizon product-automaton planner (Alg. 2-3, Sec. IV); safety follows from an n-connectivity theorem (Thm. 1), not from a runtime filter.
method: Decentralized receding-horizon planning over product automata for TWTL tasks; higher-priority neighbours' plans pruned from local search; 2H-hop communication; temporal relaxation on conflict.
evaluation: Simulation 5 agents 6x6x3 grid + 5 Crazyflie 2.0 flight test; no baseline, no ablation; only compute time reported (0.0275 s/iter at H=3, 4-core 4 GHz desktop); no collision counts.
contribution: Decentralized receding-horizon TWTL planner that provably avoids inter-agent collisions and deadlock in sufficiently connected environments, demonstrated on five quadrotors.
flag: Safety is a planner constraint with a proof, not a runtime interceptor; also fails E2 floor (no quantitative safety metric, no baseline). Real-time claim is 27.5 ms/iter on a desktop, not edge.

title: DeepMNavigate: Deep Reinforced Multi-Robot Navigation Unifying Local & Global Collision Avoidance
venue: 2020 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Policy actions are applied directly (Alg. 1, Sec. IV-C); collisions are penalised only via the training reward: 'When there is a collision, it is penalized using the function' (Sec. III-B, Eq. 4).
method: Decentralized DRL (PPO) navigation policy for differential-drive robots fed with local observations plus a rendered multi-robot motion-information map; collision avoidance learned via reward shaping.
evaluation: 2D simulation, 15-90 robots, 5 scenarios; baseline Long et al. [16]; success, stuck, collision rate, extra time; RTX 2080 Ti, ~0.25 s per step; no hardware.
contribution: DRL multi-robot navigation policy augmented with a global motion-information map, cutting collision and stuck rates versus a local-observation baseline in dense simulated crowds of up to 90 robots.
flag: Borderline (c): collision rate is measured against a baseline, but the mechanism is a reward-shaped navigation policy, not a safety mechanism (protocol v1.2); no runtime layer; simulation only.

title: Efficient Iterative Linear-Quadratic Approximations for Nonlinear Multi-Player General-Sum Differential Games
venue: 2020 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
evidence: Collision avoidance enters only as soft proximity costs in the game (Sec. V-A, proximity cost active within 1 m); 'quantitatively comparing the solutions identified by different algorithms is challenged' (Sec. VI) and no collision rates are reported.
method: Iterative linear-quadratic approximation of N-player general-sum differential games: linearize dynamics, quadraticize costs, solve coupled Riccati equations, damped update; receding-horizon re-solve.
evaluation: Simulated 3-player hallway (500 Monte Carlo inits, 5 near-contact outliers) and intersection (<0.25 s); TurtleBot 2 with two humans, replanning <50 ms; no baseline, no collision metrics.
contribution: Real-time iterative LQ approximation to multi-player general-sum differential games, solving a 14-state three-agent intersection in under 0.25 s and replanning in under 50 ms onboard a ground robot.
flag: Game-theoretic planner, no runtime interceptor; safety is a soft cost and only qualitatively shown (also E2). Humans appear as interaction partners, not as handoff recipients.

title: Efficient Multi-Agent Trajectory Planning with Feasibility Guarantee using Relative Bernstein Polynomial
venue: 2020 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
evidence: Inter-agent avoidance is a convex Relative Safe Flight Corridor constraint on Bernstein control points inside an offline QP (Sec. V); trajectories are precomputed and 'We used Crazyswarm to follow the pre-computed trajectory' (Sec. VI-D).
method: Offline multi-quadrotor trajectory planning: ECBS initial paths, safe flight corridors, relative Bernstein-polynomial corridors for pairwise avoidance, batched QP with dummy agents, feasibility guarantee (Thm. 1).
evaluation: Simulation 4-64 agents in random forests vs authors' prior method and SCP; success rate, cost, compute time (6.36 s for 64 agents, i7-7700), min-distance safety margin; 6-Crazyflie flight demo.
contribution: Offline multi-agent trajectory planner using relative Bernstein polynomials that guarantees feasible collision-free solutions and plans for 64 quadrotors in obstacle-dense space within seconds.
flag: Offline planner with collision constraints baked in; paper is about feasibility, cost and compute time; no runtime execution-time check; no closed-loop safety metric.

title: Infusing Reachability-Based Safety into Planning and Control for Multi-agent Interactions
venue: 2020 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: A low-level safety controller at 50 Hz activates when a pairwise HJ value satisfies V <= eps and solves a convex QP 'selecting feasible controls from the intersection of the safety-preserving control sets' that minimally modifies the planner's nominal command (Sec. IV-D, Eq. 12).
method: Offline HJ reachability value functions reused twice: as a planning-time reward shaping term in tree search and as a runtime minimally-interventional QP safety filter over all threatened agents.
evaluation: highway-env simulation, 100 IDM/MOBIL vehicles, 20 x 30 s episodes; baselines RSS, no controller, OP vs HJOP, MI vs SW; TTC/BTN/STN fractions, speed, intervention % (18.1% vs 57.5% RSS); 1 Hz planner / 50 Hz filter; no solve times.
contribution: Reachability-based safety infused into both planning rewards and a 50 Hz minimally interventional QP filter, matching RSS safety in dense highway traffic while intervening three times less often.
flag: Single controlled robot among 100 scripted vehicles (multi-agent hazard, but only one agent is controlled). Convexified QP loses strict HJ guarantee; no collision counts, only TTC/BTN/STN threshold fractions; simulation only, no latency figures.

title: Multi-Agent Motion Planning for Dense and Dynamic Environments via Deep Reinforcement Learning
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
evidence: 'to avoid collision in high-risk situations we propose to switch to FMP when the agent is very close to collide' - each agent at every step decides to use FMP or its learned policy based on d_min, neighbour count and a stuck counter (Sec. III-C, Alg. 1).
method: Decentralized hybrid: GA3C-CADRL-NSL learned policy as nominal controller, with a per-step runtime arbiter that overrides it with force-based motion planning (FMP) in high-risk, no-neighbour or stuck states.
evaluation: 2D/3D simulation, 2-16 agents, 50 cases per density; baselines GA3C-CADRL, NSL ablation, FMP, ORCA; collision, stuck, success rate, extra time (2D 16 agents: 24% vs 74% collisions); policy 0.4-0.5 ms on laptop GPU.
contribution: Hybrid DRL/force-based planner where a runtime distance-triggered switch overrides the learned policy with a reactive fallback, cutting collision and stuck rates in dense multi-agent simulations.
flag: Borderline (a): override is state-triggered switching to a fallback controller, not an action-level check; two of three triggers (no-neighbour, stuck) are efficiency not safety. Simulation only; 50 cases per setting.

title: Online Trajectory Generation With Distributed Model Predictive Control for Multi-Robot Motion Planning
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
evidence: Collision avoidance is a soft linear inequality constraint inside each agent's receding-horizon QP: 'we need only add an inequality constraint tuple' with slack penalised in the cost (Sec. III-E, Eqs. 10-14); 'Since the optimizer is allowed to violate the collision constraint...' (Sec. VII-A).
method: Distributed MPC with on-demand collision constraints linearised at the predicted first-collision sample, Bezier-parameterised inputs, event-triggered replanning on disturbance; run centrally off-board.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation 10-60 agents, 50 cases each, vs BVC and soft BVC; success rate (>90% to 30 agents), transition time, distance; Crazyflie swarm 2-20 drones, 9.9-20 ms QP solve, 20 Hz commands.
contribution: Online distributed MPC with on-demand linearised collision constraints that transitions up to 20 quadrotors in real time, halving transition time versus Buffered Voronoi Cells.
flag: Planner-internal soft constraints, no runtime interceptor; paper is about success/transition time/scalability; min inter-agent distance falls below r_min in hardware. Human push is a disturbance, not handoff.

title: Safe Multi-Agent Interaction through Robust Control Barrier Functions with Learned Uncertainties
venue: 2020 59th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. IV: 'u_des is any, potentially unsafe, desired control action passed to our CBF', which solves a QP projecting it to the nearest action satisfying a robust multi-agent barrier condition for every other agent; Table I: collision rate 1.5% (robust) vs 15.0% (nominal CBF).
method: Robust multi-agent control barrier function QP filter; Matrix-Variate Gaussian Process learns polytopic high-confidence bounds on other agents' dynamics uncertainty; min-max reduced to a QP.
evaluation: Simulation, 1000 randomized trials with 3-12 agents; baseline nominal multi-agent CBF; collision rate 1.5% vs 15%, distance-to-collision margins; 'real time' QP claimed, no timing or hardware reported.
contribution: Robust multi-agent CBF safety filter with GP-learned uncertainty bounds on other agents' dynamics cuts collision rate from 15% to 1.5% versus nominal CBF in simulation, with slight added conservativeness.
flag: Simulation only; real-time claim unmeasured; Gaussian-uncertainty assumption acknowledged (Remark 5); same group as 1903.07823.

title: With Whom to Communicate: Learning Efficient Communication for Multi-Robot Collision Avoidance
venue: 2020 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. IV.A: the learned policy only decides when and with whom to request trajectories; 'the resulting trajectory is constrained to not intersect with the requested and estimated trajectories' inside the NMPC, i.e. collision avoidance is a planner constraint, not an execution-time override.
method: MADDPG-trained communication policy predicts other robots' states and future collision risk to decide when/with whom to request trajectories; NMPC with collision constraints plans motion.
evaluation: Simulation (Matlab/Forces Pro, 4 quadrotors, 3 scenarios); baselines full, none and distance-based communication; metrics collisions (zero) and number of requests (~40% fewer than distance-based); no latency or hardware.
contribution: Learned when-and-with-whom communication policy for decentralized MAV collision avoidance reduces trajectory requests by about 40% versus distance-based broadcasting while keeping zero collisions in simulation.
flag: Borderline (c): collision-risk prediction drives communication, but primary claim and outcome are communication efficiency; collision avoidance lives in NMPC constraints (fails strict runtime criterion).

title: LSwarm: Efficient Collision Avoidance for Large Swarms With Coverage Constraints in Complex Urban Scenes
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
evidence: Sec. IV.B/IV.G: the preferred waypoint velocity is replaced each control cycle by the coverage-ranked velocity inside the ORCA collision-free set, which 'is guaranteed to avoid collisions'; Table III: building collisions ORCA 4/2 vs LSwarm 0 in dense models.
method: ORCA-based per-cycle velocity filter over a lawnmower waypoint controller adding static-obstacle half-planes, acceleration limits, Kalman-covariance inflation and coverage-ranked velocity selection.
evaluation: Gazebo/PX4 SITL, 20 quadrotors + 20 dynamic obstacles, 4 urban models; baseline ORCA (RVO2-3D); building collisions 4/2 vs 0, overlap ratio up to 0.89 vs 0.32; 'few ms' per step, Xeon workstation, 7x slower than ORCA.
contribution: LSwarm layers coverage-aware velocity selection on ORCA so large UAV swarms avoid buildings, dynamic obstacles and each other with zero recorded collisions and up to 2x coverage over ORCA in simulated urban scenes.
flag: Borderline: reactive local navigation planner rather than a dedicated shield; novelty is coverage preservation; collision evidence is building-collision counts only (Table III); workstation timing, no onboard measurement.

title: Learning Safe Unlabeled Multi-Robot Planning with Motion Constraints
venue: 2019 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Sec. III-D / Algorithm 1 step 5: if the learned actor's velocity lies inside the velocity obstacle it is projected to the nearest safe velocity before execution ('a simple analytical backup policy that ensures collision free trajectories'); Table I: collisions 84/192/354 (MARL) vs 0 (MARL+RVO) over 500 runs.
method: MADDPG-style multi-agent RL for concurrent goal assignment and trajectory planning with a velocity-obstacle projection backup filter (smooth sigmoid in training, hard min-projection at inference).
evaluation: 2D simulation, 3-5 robots, 500 runs; baselines vanilla MARL, RVO, GAP, centralized PPO; metrics collisions (0 vs up to 354), time to goal; DGX-1 training time only, no inference latency.
contribution: Velocity-obstacle projection shield on a MARL policy for unlabeled multi-robot planning eliminates collisions (0 vs 84-354 over 500 runs) at near-comparable mission time to classical planners in simulation.
flag: Simulation only; 'almost safe' wording in intro and no formal proof of the min projection; Sec. V overstates speed relative to reported results.

title: Learning Vision-Based Flight in Drone Swarms by Imitation
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
evidence: Sec. IV-A: the network's predicted velocity commands are sent to the agents 'in their raw form without any further processing'; collision avoidance is learned by imitating a Reynolds flocking expert (Sec. III-A), with no execution-time filter.
method: DAgger-style imitation of a Reynolds flocking expert by a small CNN on omnidirectional images, with unsupervised domain adaptation and motion-capture refinement for real flights.
evaluation: Gazebo with 9 drones vs position-based flocking baseline (min/max inter-agent distances); 2 real quadrotors with Jetson TX1 onboard, single representative flights; 'real-time onboard' claimed, no latency measured.
contribution: Vision-only decentralized drone flocking learned by imitation of a position-based flocking expert, transferred to two real quadrotors with onboard inference via unsupervised domain adaptation.
flag: Human stops data-collection flights when 'subjectively too dangerous' (training-time only, not (e)); no quantitative collision metric vs baseline, so also E2.

title: Safe Policy Synthesis in Multi-Agent POMDPs via Discrete-Time Barrier Functions
venue: 2019 IEEE 58th Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Sec. IV-A, Algorithm 3: the nominal policy's joint action is applied if the predicted belief update satisfies the discrete-time barrier condition; otherwise the filter selects the safe joint action that 'minimally changes the immediate reward'.
method: Discrete-time barrier functions on the joint belief of a multi-agent POMDP, with Boolean composition; one-step greedy safe controller or safety filter wrapping a nominal planning policy.
evaluation: ROS simulation, 3 heterogeneous robots, 125 joint actions; nominal near-optimal policy vs filtered policy, qualitative trajectories only (95% habitable-cell requirement); no metrics, hardware or timing.
contribution: Discrete-time barrier functions over the joint belief yield an online safety filter for multi-agent POMDPs that overrides a nominal planning policy whenever the next belief would violate a probabilistic safety set.
flag: Method squarely meets (a) and (c) but evaluation is a single qualitative case study with no collision/violation rate; maintainer may want to check for a quantitative journal extension; infeasibility (no safe action) not addressed.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning Framework Towards Multi-Agent Navigation
venue: 2018 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Biomimetics (ROBIO)
evidence: Sec. III.C/III.D: collision avoidance is learned via a post-collision penalty in the DRL reward and an HMM hazard score that merely weights the target-driven and avoidance controller outputs (Eq. 9); nothing is vetoed or halted at execution time.
method: Hierarchical navigation (HNRN): HMM scores laser perception to weight a differential target-driven controller against a DRL collision-avoidance policy; decentralized, 2D laser only.
evaluation: Gazebo/ROS TurtleBot3, 2-32 agents; baselines ORCA, supervised policy, RL [21], plus training-variant ablation; success rate 0.941 vs 0.867/0.850 at 20 agents, collision rate, time, path length; no compute time or hardware.
contribution: HNRN hierarchical HMM-plus-DRL navigation decouples target seeking from collision avoidance, improving success rate over ORCA and end-to-end RL in simulated multi-agent crowds of up to 32 robots.
flag: Navigation planner; collision rate is one metric among success/time/path length and primary claim is training efficiency and success rate (fails primacy test).

title: Towards Optimally Decentralized Multi-Robot Collision Avoidance via Deep Reinforcement Learning
venue: 2018 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
evidence: Collision avoidance is learned via a reward penalty r_collision=-15 when a robot is too close to another robot or obstacle (Sec. IV-A, Eq. 6); the policy outputs velocity commands directly with no interception or fallback.
method: Decentralized sensor-level DRL policy (laser scans to velocity) trained with multi-scenario multi-stage policy gradient (PPO-style trust region) for multi-robot collision avoidance.
evaluation: Stage simulation, 4-100 robots; baselines NH-ORCA and supervised-learning policy plus stage-1 ablation; success rate (collision-free arrival), extra time/distance, speed; 3 ms CPU / 1.3 ms GPU inference for 10 robots.
contribution: Shows a decentralized sensor-level DRL navigation policy that reaches higher collision-free success rates than NH-ORCA in simulation with up to 100 robots, but offers no runtime safety layer.
flag: Borderline (c): collision-free success rate vs NH-ORCA is a primary metric, but the contribution is a navigation policy with safety only as a reward term, no detector/certificate; maintainer may judge primacy differently. Extended journal version exists (Fan et al. 2020, IJRR).

title: Decentralized non-communicating multiagent collision avoidance with deep reinforcement learning
venue: 2017 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
evidence: Reward penalizes the agent for getting too close or colliding with the other agent (Sec. II-B, Eq. 5); actions are chosen by one-step lookahead over a learned value network (Alg. 1), with no runtime filter.
method: CADRL: offline-trained value network over joint two-agent state; online greedy action selection against learned value; n>2 handled by approximation.
evaluation: Simulation only, 2-8 agents; baseline ORCA and CADRL-with-constraints variant; metrics extra time to goal and average min separation; i7-5820K Python, 5.7 ms/iter (2 agents), 62 ms (10 agents).
contribution: Introduces CADRL, a decentralized non-communicating collision-avoidance policy that moves interaction prediction offline and reduces time-to-goal by over 26% versus ORCA in simulation.
flag: Primary metric is path quality (extra time); no collision rate reported; safety only via reward shaping.

title: Deep-Learned Collision Avoidance Policy for Distributed Multiagent Navigation
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
evidence: Supervised policy trained on ORCA labels; the only online check slows the velocity if it would collide with static obstacles (Sec. IV-C.3), inter-agent avoidance is implicit in the learned policy.
method: CANet: end-to-end supervised deep network mapping noisy sensor readings to velocity classes, trained on ORCA-generated multi-agent simulation data.
evaluation: Six simulated scenarios averaged over 20 runs plus qualitative real-robot demo; baseline ORCA (two radii); travel time, distance, safety margin, failure rate (2% vs 15% L-shape); Titan X training; no inference time.
contribution: Learns a distributed multi-agent navigation policy from ORCA demonstrations that tolerates noisy sensing, trading smaller safety margins for shorter paths than ORCA in simulation.
flag: Navigation policy evaluated on path quality; obstacle-only velocity slow-down is a minor post-processing step, not a multi-agent safety filter; real-robot results qualitative only.

title: Safe open-loop strategies for handling intermittent communications in multi-robot systems
venue: 2017 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
evidence: On communication failure each robot executes the last received velocity command for the corresponding safe time horizon and 'Beyond the safe time horizon, the robot stops moving' (Sec. IV, Alg. 1).
method: Central decision maker computes per-robot safe time horizons from ellipsoidal over-approximations of pairwise reachable sets; robots run open-loop then halt when the horizon expires.
evaluation: Simulation with 6 robots and 4 Khepera III robots with OptiTrack; baseline stop-on-failure; qualitative trajectory plots only, no collision or completion statistics, no compute time.
contribution: Proposes provably safe open-loop fallback for centrally commanded robot teams: each robot carries a safe time horizon after which it halts, bridging intermittent communication without inter-robot collisions.
flag: Conceptually close to RQ2 (safe time horizon is a time-to-irreversibility budget before a halt) but evaluation is purely qualitative with no quantitative safety metric.

title: Multi-objective compositions for collision-free connectivity maintenance in teams of mobile robots
venue: 2016 IEEE 55th Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
evidence: Experiments 'wrapped around the nominal waypoint controller using the QP-based strategy (21)' that minimally modifies the nominal input subject to a composed barrier constraint (Sec. IV-B, V).
method: Boolean (AND/OR) compositions of control barrier functions for collision avoidance and connectivity, enforced by a QP safety filter that minimally alters a nominal controller.
evaluation: Four Khepera robots with OptiTrack/ROS, waypoint tasks designed to collide; no quantitative baseline or ablation; inter-robot distance plots against 0.15 m / 0.6 m thresholds; no solver time.
contribution: Composes collision-avoidance and connectivity barrier functions with logical operators and enforces them through a QP filter wrapped around a nominal controller on a four-robot team.
flag: Runtime QP filter clearly meets (a) and (c), but evidence is distance plots from single hardware runs with no collision counts, trials or baseline; same group as 1609.00651.

title: Obstacle avoidance via B-spline parametrizations of flat trajectories
venue: 2016 24th Mediterranean Conference on Control and Automation (MED)
evidence: Trajectory generation is solved offline over B-spline control points and 'online only a straightforward trajectory tracking is employed' (Sec. I); inter-agent avoidance 'is similar and not depicted here' (Sec. V).
method: Differential-flatness trajectory generation with B-spline parametrization; separating-hyperplane constraints on control-point convex hulls give continuous-time obstacle avoidance, exact and mixed-integer variants.
evaluation: Single simulated 2D fixed-wing scenario with three obstacles; compares no avoidance, nonlinear exact and mixed-integer formulations; metrics computation time and path length; MATLAB/YALMIP/IPOPT, hardware unreported.
contribution: Encodes obstacle avoidance as hyperplane constraints on B-spline control points so flat trajectories remain collision-free in continuous time, evaluated offline on a simulated aerial vehicle.
flag: Offline planning constraint, single-agent evaluation only; multi-agent case stated but not evaluated.

title: Provably safe and deadlock-free execution of multi-robot plans under delaying disturbances
venue: 2016 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: At each step control law G_i decides whether robot i advances or halts, allowing it 'to proceed only if the line segment' to the next point avoids coordination-space collision regions with robots behind it (Sec. III-B, Eq. 1).
method: RMTRACK: runtime execution policy that gates each robot's advancement along pre-planned multi-robot trajectories using coordination-space collision regions, provably safe and deadlock-free under delaying disturbances.
evaluation: Simulation in three environments, 10-50 robots, 10 instances, disturbance 0-50%; baselines ALLSTOP and ORCA; metrics travel time vs analytic bound, success rate (ORCA deadlocks); no hardware or compute time.
contribution: RMTRACK gates robot advancement along jointly planned trajectories so execution stays collision-free and deadlock-free under stochastic delays, at far lower travel-time cost than halting the whole team.
flag: Collision-freeness is proven rather than measured (no collision counts); quantitative outcomes are travel-time overhead and success rate vs ALLSTOP/ORCA, which speak to RQ5 (cost of halts). Humans appear only as exogenous disturbances. Maintainer should confirm success rate counts as a safety metric.

title: Safety barrier certificates for heterogeneous multi-robot systems
venue: 2016 American Control Conference (ACC)
evidence: The barrier certificate 'takes over and computes the closest permissible control in a least-squares sense when collision is about to happen' and is 'executed as a lower level safety program' below the nominal controller (Sec. III-A, VI).
method: Pairwise control barrier functions for heterogeneous double-integrator robots with differing acceleration limits, enforced by a minimally invasive QP; decentralized variant and local estimation of unknown neighbor dynamics.
evaluation: MATLAB simulation with six heterogeneous agents and experiment with three Khepera III plus one Magellan Pro under OptiTrack; no quantitative baseline or ablation; trajectory plots only; no compute time.
contribution: Extends safety barrier certificates to heterogeneous robot teams with unknown neighbor dynamics, filtering nominal commands through a QP that intervenes only when collision is imminent.
flag: Runtime QP filter meets (a) and (c) but safety evidence is qualitative trajectory plots; the only comparison is the statement that the unfiltered controller would collide. Companion to 1608.06887; later Wang et al. T-RO 2017 journal version may be in queue.
